function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content:
Below is a quick “cheat‑sheet” of some of the most popular **object‑detection** models that you can pull straight from TorchHub (i.e., `torch.hub.load`). I’ll give you: * The repository name (`repo_id`) you pass to `torch.hub.load` * The model name (`model_name`) you pass as the second argument * A short description / typical use case * A minimal code snippet that shows how to load the model and run inference on a single image Feel free to copy/paste the snippets into your own script – they’re ready to run (assuming you have PyTorch installed). --- ## 1️⃣ torchvision (official PyTorch repo) | Model | Repo ID | Description | Code | |-------|---------|-------------|------| | **Faster R‑CNN (ResNet‑50 backbone)** | `pytorch/vision:v0.13.1` | Classic two‑stage detector, good accuracy, slower | ```python
import torch, torchvision
model = torch.hub.load('pytorch/vision:v0.13.1', 'fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn', pretrained=True)
model.eval()
# Inference example:
from PIL import Image
img = Image.open('image.jpg').convert('RGB')
transform = torchvision.transforms.ToTensor()
tensor = transform(img).unsqueeze(0) # add batch dim
with torch.no_grad():\n predictions = model(tensor)[0] # dict with boxes, labels, scores\n``` | | **RetinaNet (ResNet‑50 backbone)** | `pytorch/vision:v0.13.1` | One‑stage detector, fast, decent accuracy | ```python
model = torch.hub.load('pytorch/vision:v0.13.1', 'retinanet_resnet50_fpn', pretrained=True)
model.eval()
... # same inference pattern as above
``` | | **SSD300 (VGG‑16 backbone)** | `pytorch/vision:v0.13.1` | Very fast, lower accuracy | ```python
model = torch.hub.load('pytorch/vision:v0.13.1', 'ssd300_vgg16', pretrained=True)
model.eval()
... # same inference pattern
``` | > **Tip:** Use `torch.hub.list('pytorch/vision:v0.13.1')` to see all available models in that repo. --- ## 2️⃣ Ultralytics YOLOv5 (YOLO family) | Model | Repo ID | Description | Code | |-------|---------|-------------|------| | **YOLOv5s** (smallest) | `ultralytics/yolov5` | Fast, lightweight, great for edge devices | ```python
model = torch.hub.load('ultralytics/yolov5', 'yolov5s', pretrained=True)
model.eval()
results = model('image.jpg') # returns a Results object
print(results.xyxy[0]) # bounding boxes + confidence + class id
``` | | **YOLOv5m** | `ultralytics/yolov5`, `'yolov5m'` | Medium trade‑off between speed & accuracy | ```python
model = torch.hub.load('ultralytics/yolov5', 'yolov5m', pretrained=True)
...
``` | | **YOLOv5l** | `ultralytics/yolov5`, `'yolov5l'` | Larger, more accurate | ```python
model = torch.hub.load('ultralytics/yolov5', 'yolov5l', pretrained=True)
...
``` | | **YOLOv5x** | `ultralytics/yolov5`, `'yolov5x'` | Largest, best accuracy | ```python
model = torch.hub.load('ultralytics/yolov5', 'yolov5x', pretrained=True)
...
``` | > **Note:** YOLOv5’s `Results` object has handy methods: `.plot()`, `.save()`, `.pandas().xyxy[0]`, etc. --- ## 3️⃣ Detectron2 (Facebook AI Research) Detectron2 is not part of the official `torch.hub` registry, but you can still load it via a custom repo ID: ```python model = torch.hub.load( 'facebookresearch/detectron2', 'detectron2_repo', source='github', force_reload=False, trust_repo=True ) ``` Once loaded, you’d typically use the Detectron2 API (`DefaultPredictor`, `setup_cfg`, etc.) rather than raw TorchHub calls. See the [Detectron2 docs](https://detectron2.readthedocs.io/) for full usage. --- ## 4️⃣ Other community repos | Repo | Model | How to load | |------|-------|-------------| | `NVIDIA/DeepLearningExamples` | `ssd_mobilenet_v2_coco` | `torch.hub.load('NVIDIA/DeepLearningExamples', 'ssd_mobilenet_v2_coco', pretrained=True)` | | `NVIDIA/DeepLearningExamples` | `faster_rcnn_inception_resnet_v2_atrous_coco` | `torch.hub.load('NVIDIA/DeepLearningExamples', 'faster_rcnn_inception_resnet_v2_atrous_coco', pretrained=True)` | | `NVIDIA/DeepLearningExamples` | `mask_rcnn_inception_resnet_v2_atrous_coco` | `torch.hub.load('NVIDIA/DeepLearningExamples', 'mask_rcnn_inception_resnet_v2_atrous_coco', pretrained=True)` | > These NVIDIA models often come with extra utilities (e.g., `predictor.py`) that simplify inference. --- ## 5️⃣ Quick sanity check: List all models in a repo If you’re curious what else is available, run: ```python import torch print(torch.hub.list('pytorch/vision:v0.13.1')) # prints all torchvision models print(torch.hub.list('ultralytics/yolov5')) # prints all YOLOv5 variants ``` --- ### Putting it together – a minimal demo ```python import torch from PIL import Image import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np # Load a YOLOv5s model model = torch.hub.load('ultralytics/yolov5', 'yolov5s', pretrained=True) model.eval() # Read an image img_path = 'image.jpg' img = Image.open(img_path).convert('RGB') # Run inference results = model(img) # results is a Results object df = results.pandas().xyxy[0] # pandas DataFrame with detections # Visualize fig, ax = plt.subplots(1) ax.imshow(np.array(img)) for _, row in df.iterrows(): xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = int(row['xmin']), int(row['ymin']), int(row['xmax']), int(row['ymax']) rect = plt.Rectangle((xmin, ymin), xmax - xmin, ymax - ymin, linewidth=2, edgecolor='r', facecolor='none') ax.add_patch(rect) ax.text(xmin, ymin - 5, f"{row['name']} {row['confidence']:.2f}", color='white', fontsize=12, backgroundcolor='red') plt.show() ``` That’s it! You now have a handful of ready‑to‑use object‑detection models pulled directly from TorchHub. Pick the one that best matches your speed/accuracy needs, drop it into your pipeline, and start detecting objects in minutes. Happy coding!
